## Setup and computers

**I have Windows. Can I take part?** Yes, through WSL2 (a real Linux inside
Windows) or GitHub Codespaces. Three tools of the pipeline (`bwa`, `samtools`,
`bcftools`) have no Windows builds, so native Windows only works for the
report and notebook lessons. See [setup](pages/00-setup.qmd).

**My laptop is old or locked down.** Use a Codespace (setup, step 7). The free
quota (about 60 hours a month on a 2-core machine) is enough for the course if
you stop codespaces when you are done.

**How much disk space do I need?** About 10 GB free: roughly 4 GB of software
environments for the example project, 0.5 GB of data and results, and Pixi's
package cache. [Take-down](pages/B-take-down.qmd) frees it afterwards.

**I have never used a terminal. Is that a problem?** No. The lessons give
every command, but they go faster if `cd`, `ls` and pipes are familiar. Spend
an hour on [Bash 101](pages/C-bash.qmd) before lesson 02; it ends with
longer shell tutorials, from Data Carpentry and Software Carpentry, if you
want more.

**Do I need administrator rights?** Not for Pixi or anything it installs. Only
WSL2 (Windows) and Docker need them, once.

## Tools

**Why Pixi and not Conda?** Pixi uses the same packages (conda-forge,
bioconda), but keeps the environment in the project, always writes a lock
file for every platform, and runs tasks. That makes "rebuild exactly what I
used" one command. Conda is still covered:
[05b Pixi and Conda compared](pages/05b-conda-comparison.qmd).

**Why Python and not R?** To keep one language across Quarto, Jupyter and the
helper scripts. Everything in the course works the same with R: Quarto runs
R, and Pixi installs R packages from conda-forge.

**Why both Snakemake and Nextflow?** They are the two main workflow managers
in bioinformatics; you will meet both. Snakemake is taught in full; Nextflow
gets an introduction and a home tutorial on the same pipeline, so you can
compare them, and their results are identical.

**Do I need to understand the genomics?** No. The variant-calling steps come
from the Data Carpentry lesson and are treated as a given pipeline. The course
is about making any analysis reproducible.

## The course material

**Can I use this material in my own teaching?** Yes: text and slides are
CC BY 4.0 and code is MIT. Credit the workshop and the sources it adapts
([Sources and credits](pages/credits.qmd)), and say what you changed.

**I found a mistake.** Please open an issue or a pull request on the
[GitHub repository](https://github.com/khan-lab/cbio7501-f26).

**How are the tutorials tested?** Every shell command in a tutorial is
marked in the source and run by `pixi run test-tutorials` in a fresh folder,
lesson after lesson, as a learner would. GitHub Actions runs them on Linux and
macOS after every change and every Monday, including the Git and Docker steps
(Linux); the [latest runs](https://github.com/khan-lab/cbio7501-f26/actions)
show whether they pass today. Steps that need your own accounts (GitHub web
pages, Zenodo) or a cluster are not tested automatically.
